reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile is almost uniformly elite: .413 xwOBA, 17.2% barrel rate, 93.4 mph average exit velocity, and a 14.3% walk rate that turns even the contact questions into a minor footnote. The contact questions are genuine, a 28.9% whiff rate that sits well below average, but a hitter putting that much force on contact at that walk rate absorbs a lot of strikeout variance without meaningful damage to the projection's .393 OBP. On the mound, a 2.71 xERA and 98.1 mph fastball with 2486 rpm of spin frame a pitcher who misses bats at a 30.4% whiff rate and holds barrels to just 3.8%. The whole thing hinges on health and innings load, which is the only scenario where both sides of this profile don't translate into something that belongs in a separate conversation from almost every other player at this level.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .428 xwOBA and 22.4% barrel rate both sit at the 100th percentile, and the .607 xSLG says the raw power is translating. The 29.6% strikeout rate is almost exactly the tax you pay for it, but what holds the profile together is the 17.1% walk rate: he's genuinely hard to put away, and a 22.5% chase rate confirms pitchers can't expand the zone to solve him. If the strikeout rate stays near where it is, this is a .266/.388/.530 line with 41 home runs, a true middle-of-the-order bat. If he ever finds enough in-zone contact to close the gap between his .277 xBA and his actual hit tool, the ceiling gets uncomfortable fast.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .307, 99th percentile, and the contact quality underneath it is just as loud: 92.9 mph average exit velocity, 52.2% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .518. Those three numbers describe a hitter who does genuine damage when he connects, and a 17.5% strikeout rate says he connects plenty. The one real tension in the profile is a 33.2% chase rate that lives in the bottom third of the league, meaning the raw contact talent is doing heavy lifting against a discipline number that could get exploited if pitchers find a consistent edge-and-off approach. If the chase rate stabilizes around its current level and doesn't climb, the projection's .283/.351/.471 with 45 stolen bags is an easy floor, not a ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs and 39 steals in the same projection season is a combination that almost nobody produces, and the Statcast profile explains the mechanism. His 48.3% hard-hit rate pairs with a .357 xwOBA that reflects contact quality baked into where and how hard the ball is leaving the bat. The concern is specific: a 35.6% chase rate and 26.5% strikeout rate that rank near the bottom of the league, meaning the offensive ceiling depends on pitchers not solving him before he adjusts. If they do, you still have one of the fastest players in baseball at 29.5 ft/s and elite defense in center, which keeps the floor from cratering — but the 32-homer, 39-steal version only lives if the chase rate doesn't get him killed.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.76 and the strikeout rate is 29.7%, and both are doing exactly what you'd expect from a guy holding opposing contact to a 6.1% barrel rate while walking just 5.6% of batters. That combination, miss bats, limit free passes, suppress damage when contact happens, is the cleanest formula in pitching, and Skenes executes all three. At 187.2 innings with 226 strikeouts and a 1.05 WHIP, the workload-plus-efficiency line is the kind that wins Cy Young votes. The one thing to watch is whether the 27.8% whiff rate, modest relative to the rest of the profile, firms up as hitters accumulate looks at the arsenal; if the chase rate at 33.9% starts to soften, the strikeout volume follows.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here has a real split personality. His 53.5% hard-hit rate puts him in rarefied air for pure contact quality, yet a 28.7% whiff rate bleeds enough of that value away that the xwOBA lands at .354, solid but not elite. The speed is genuine, 28.9 ft/s at the 90th percentile, and 38 projected steals tell you the legs are still a weapon even after everything. What the projection (.280/.351/.421) is really saying is that this is a plus-tools player whose floor keeps getting set by swing-and-miss, and if the whiff rate doesn't tighten from where it sits, the power (.421 SLG against an xSLG of .440) never fully arrives either.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact profile and the strikeout rate are pulling in opposite directions, and that's the whole argument. A 94.4 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, the barrel rate is 14.9%, and yet a 27.4% strikeout rate drags the ceiling down — he's leaving runs on the field every time he swings through a pitch he could barrel. The .367 xwOBA says the underlying quality is genuinely elite when he makes contact, and the projection translates that into a .273/.347/.490 line with 27 home runs and 28 stolen bases, which is a legitimate star season. The profile hinges entirely on whether the strikeout rate stays at that level or creeps higher, because if the swing-and-miss ticks up, you lose plate appearances and the counting stats shrink fast, and what's left is a high-variance middle-of-the-order bat who is thrilling on his best nights and frustrating everywhere else.

reports.name: Trea Turner
reports.published_report: The legs are the argument and the problem at the same time. At 29.9 ft/s he sits at the 98th percentile in sprint speed, and 28 projected stolen bases across 697 plate appearances are the clearest path to value left in this profile. But a .294 xwOBA grades 19th percentile, a 35.2% chase rate grades 20th, and a 6.3% walk rate sits near the bottom of the discipline spectrum, a combination that turns a once-legitimate middle-of-the-order bat into something closer to a second-division regular. The whole thing hinges on whether the speed stays healthy enough to keep the stolen-base number meaningful, because the contact and power numbers, .252/.303/.391 in projection, do not carry him on their own.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert

Gilbert doesn't miss as many bats as a true frontline arm, but a 30.3% whiff rate and 33.7% chase rate give him enough to work with, and because he almost never gives the free pass, hitters have to swing and live with the consequences. reports.name: Cody Bellinger
reports.published_report: The .276 xBA with a 12.6% walk rate tells you most of what you need to know: Bellinger's actual production lags his contact quality because he doesn't hit the ball particularly hard, 36.8% hard-hit rate and a 6.5% barrel rate both sitting in the bottom third of the league. What he does instead is make a lot of contact on the right pitches, whiff on just 20.3% of swings, and take enough walks that a .340 OBP is genuinely supported. The projection's 21 home runs feel like the ceiling on the power, not the floor, and if the exit velocity doesn't tick up, .427 SLG is about where the ceiling sits too. A league-average everyday player with real on-base skills and a Fielding OAA that grades out elite — that's a useful piece, just not the middle-of-the-order force the Yankees might be hoping for.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 183 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the loudest thing in this profile. Across AAA & A+ & A in 2026, Jenkins is striking out just 15% of the time against a 13% walk rate, and those translate to an MLB-equivalent K% of 18.9 against a league figure of 22.0, with a 10.4% walk rate against the 8.5% norm. That's a disciplined left-handed hitter who makes the ball find his barrel, not one who survives on athleticism. The .202 ISO across those 200 plate appearances is modest but honest — the .153 MLB-equivalent ISO sits essentially at league average, so the ceiling here runs through contact and on-base value rather than over-the-fence power. If the strike-zone feel translates and the hit tool plays at the highest level, this is an everyday center fielder; if the power stays suppressed and the contact erodes even a little, you're looking at a second-division regular with a real glove.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: An 18.3% chase rate ranks at the 99th percentile, and that's the whole architecture of this profile. McGonigle doesn't punish pitchers with raw exit velocity, 87.9 mph average is well below the MLB mean, but he earns contact so cleanly through plate discipline that his xwOBA sits at .363, with an xSLG of .444 that the projection trusts more than the hard-hit numbers would suggest. The argument for him is that a 14.3% walk rate against a 13.8% strikeout rate makes him nearly impossible to beat by expanding the zone, and hitters who live in the strike zone age well. If the power-to-contact tradeoff holds at this extreme, the projection (.276/.379/.424, 16 home runs) looks like a real everyday player at third or short; if the exit velocity gap closes off development, what's left is a high-OBP second-division regular whose stolen base threat keeps the floor interesting.

reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: Thirty projected home runs from a shortstop who barrels the ball at a 13.0% clip is a genuine weapon, and that barrel rate sits well above the middle of the league while everything else in the contact profile is quietly alarming. A 31.4% strikeout rate and a 36.4% chase rate explain why his xBA lands at .203, which is about as low as a hitter can go before the batting average starts costing him lineup time. The disconnect between an 83rd-percentile barrel rate and a 4th-percentile xBA is the whole tension here: he hits the ball hard enough to matter when he makes contact, but he's chasing too often to make contact consistently. If the chase rate comes down even a few ticks, the power is already calibrated and the projection's .321 OBP starts to feel conservative; if it doesn't, the strikeouts keep the batting average buried and he's a volatile middle-of-the-order tease rather than a cornerstone.

reports.name: Max Clark
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 385 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power ratio is the whole tension here: Max Clark is making contact at a level that translates comfortably to the majors, but the bat lacks the damage to match. His 15% strikeout rate at AAA translates to 18.3% at the MLB level, noticeably cleaner than most hitters face, and 44 walks in 385 plate appearances show genuine zone feel. The power, though, is the limiting factor — a .14 ISO at AAA translates to .125 at the MLB level, well short of the 150-point MLB average, and 8 home runs in 385 PA don't suggest that gap closes without a mechanical shift. The 20 stolen bases buy real value if the hit tool stays clean, and a .353 OBP at 21 years old is a floor worth respecting. He's either a low-end everyday center fielder if the speed and contact age well together, or a capable bench piece if the power ceiling holds where it sits right now.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics don't belong to the same player, except they do. A 96.0 mph average exit velocity and 16.7% barrel rate that would make any evaluator drool sit right next to a 37.8% whiff rate and 34.6% K%, both at the bottom of the league. The question isn't whether Cruz can hit the ball hard; 59.2% hard-hit rate settles that. It's whether he makes contact often enough for that violence to matter, and the projection answer is .252/.339/.456 with 21 home runs and 31 stolen bases in 455 plate appearances: sometimes, and enough to be valuable, but this is a feast-or-famine profile that lives or dies by his at-bat quality in two-strike counts. If the chase rate at 32.4% creeps up and the walks at 10.6% dry up, the power doesn't disappear but the counting stats do, and you're left with a high-strikeout, low-average regular who costs you lineup continuity more than he builds it.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: The fastball sits at 97.5 mph and hitters barrel it only 5.3% of the time, which tells you why contact against him stays manageable even when he doesn't miss many bats. That 18.8% strikeout rate and 21.8% whiff rate are genuinely modest for a front-line starter, but the walk rate at 6.5% is better than most of the rotation in this league, and the combination keeps his xERA at 3.69. Alcantara's profile is a contact-manager first, beating you with the fastball's quality and his ability to avoid barrels rather than with swing-and-miss, and the 209.9 projected innings confirm the durability is still the asset. If the barrel suppression slips, there isn't a strikeout rate deep enough to pick up the slack.

reports.name: Eury Pérez
reports.published_report: The fastball is 98.2 mph with 2665 rpm of spin, and that combination is what everything else in this profile is waiting on. The 28.0% strikeout rate is legitimate, the 28.8% whiff rate is above average, and the chase numbers are solid enough that when hitters do swing, he's getting them off balance. The problem is 10.0% walks, which explains why the xERA sits at 4.05 despite all that swing-and-miss: the stuff generates contact quality that's roughly league-average, and the free passes keep him from pulling away. If Pérez learns to throw that heater in the zone without making it hittable, still a big if at 22, the projection's 3.68 ERA over 145.7 innings is credible; if the command stalls at its current level, you're watching a young arm with loud stuff that beats itself.

Bradley's 27.2 K% grades well above league average, but his 45.3% hard-hit rate and 9.8% barrel rate sit near the bottom of the league, and a 29.2% chase rate explains the shape: he misses bats inside the zone rather than getting hitters to chase, so when contact happens it tends to be damaging. The 96.9 mph fastball earns the whiffs, but the profile hinges on whether he can start pushing hitters off the plate enough to change that contact quality. If the chase rate climbs, the 3.91 xERA and a projected 174.5 innings start to look like a mid-rotation arm settling in; if it doesn't, he's accumulating strikeouts while absorbing hard contact, which is a workable but fragile way to pitch.

reports.name: Foster Griffin
reports.published_report: The 3.88 xERA says league-average results, and that's being kind to the stuff — 91.5 mph fastball sitting at the 9th percentile, spin to match. What keeps him functional is command: a 5.7% walk rate that grades out at the 90th percentile, paired with a 33.6% chase rate that does real work getting hitters to expand. The projection's 3.08 ERA and 181.5 innings hinge entirely on that chase rate continuing to manufacture weak contact, because when hitters stop chasing, there's no swing-and-miss profile to fall back on. Floor-to-ceiling, this is a back-end starter who stays useful exactly as long as the command and deception hold.

reports.name: Angel Genao
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with low risk. The current bat shape is impact over 246 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The plate discipline is doing the heavy lifting here. Across AAA & AA this season, Genao has walked 52 times against 55 strikeouts in 356 plate appearances, and the MLB translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.8% against a league that averages 22.0% — contact that travels with him. The power reads as below-average at that level, with a translated ISO of .139 against a .150 MLB norm, so the .294/.399/.463 line across AAA & AA is built more on getting on base than hitting it over the fence. If the contact profile holds and his 8 stolen bases hint at enough speed to add value at short, you're looking at a low-end everyday regular; if the power stalls and the strikeout rate creeps up against big-league arms, what's left is a useful bench piece with a good eye.

reports.name: Casey Mize
reports.published_report: The xERA sitting at 3.14 is the number that matters, and it holds up because the walk rate does the heavy lifting: 5.9% BB% is genuinely elite command, and when a pitcher limits free passes that cleanly, contact quality becomes almost secondary. The Whiff% at 29.2% is above average without being a strikeout weapon — 25.6% K% is solid but not the story. What Mize actually is, based on the Statcast profile, is a command-over-stuff arm who gets outs through location and contact management rather than overwhelming hitters, which makes the 93.6 mph fastball a non-issue as long as the precision holds. The projection settling at a 3.25 ERA over 139.8 innings looks like a fair translation of a guy who was quietly one of the better starters in the AL when healthy; the whole profile hinges on staying in the rotation, because abbreviated on the IL, that command-driven floor doesn't look like anything useful.

That tension is the whole profile. The projection resolves it honestly, landing at .248/.305/.414 with 21 home runs, which is a functional everyday infielder who gets to his counting stats through volume and modest contact quality rather than any one carrying tool. The floor hinges on that 33.5% chase rate: if pitchers punish it and the contact advantage narrows, what's left is a .719 OPS guy without a walk rate to compensate.

reports.name: Reid Detmers
reports.published_report: The Statcast card and the projection don't quite agree on Detmers, and that gap is the whole read. His xERA sits at 3.26 and his xwOBA at .281, both in the 80th percentile, while the projection lands at a 4.05 ERA over 179.4 innings. The difference lives almost entirely in his fastball spin at 2154 rpm, a 20th-percentile reading that suggests hitters will keep squaring him up when the secondary stuff isn't working, even if contact quality at 89.6 mph average exit velocity runs modest. The strikeout rate is legitimate, 27.4% with a 28.7% whiff rate and 200 projected punchouts over a full workload, but if his walks creep up from an already middling 7.4%, the ERA drifts toward the uglier end of what's projected rather than toward what the expected metrics imply. The profile is a mid-rotation arm who might pitch like a front-of-rotation arm in his best stretches, held back by a fastball that doesn't miss enough bats on its own.

reports.name: Clayton Beeter
reports.published_report: Twenty saves projected for a reliever with a 1.35 WHIP is a tension worth sitting with. The spin rate is the real engine here — 2410 rpm on the fastball puts him in the 83rd percentile, which explains why a 95.5 mph heater plays up and gets swings-and-misses that the velocity alone wouldn't generate, and 61 projected strikeouts over 53.2 innings confirms the pitch earns its keep. If the command sharpens and that WHIP comes down, he's a genuine multi-inning closer option in Washington; if the walks stay elevated and hitters adjust to the heater, the save total shrinks and the profile flattens into a hold-accumulator.
